extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, toxicologists, safety assessors, regulatory classifiers, SDS/labelling preparers
extracted.subtask_short: GHS skin and eye hazard classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for classifying substances and mixtures for skin corrosion/irritation and serious eye damage/eye irritation under GHS-style criteria, including tiered evaluation, test method preferences, mixture bridging/ additivity rules, pH-based rules, and cut-off concentration thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion from acute toxicity categories to point estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Table A.1.2—Conversion From Experimentally Obtained Acute Toxicity Range Values (or Acute Toxicity Hazard Categories) to Acute Toxicity Point Estimates for Use in the Formulas for the Classification of Mixtures
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides converted acute toxicity point estimates for various exposure routes and experimentally obtained ranges/category boundaries (oral, dermal, gases (ppmV), vapors (mg/l), dust/mist (mg/l)). Example entries: Oral: 0 < Category 1 ≤ 5 → 0.5 mg/kg; 5 < Category 2 ≤ 50 → 5 mg/kg; Dermal: 0 < Category 1 ≤ 50 → 5 mg/kg; Gases: 0 < Category 1 ≤ 100 → 10 ppmV; Vapors: 0 < Category 1 ≤ 0.5 → 0.05 mg/l; Dust/mist: 0 < Category 1 ≤ 0.05 → 0.005 mg/l. (See table for full mapping.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling ingredients of unknown acute toxicity in mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: If an ingredient with unknown acute toxicity is used in a mixture at a concentration ≥1%, and the mixture has not been classified based on testing of the mixture as a whole, the mixture cannot be attributed a definitive acute toxicity estimate and is classified based on the known ingredients only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement that × percent of the mixture consists of ingredient(s) of unknown acute (oral/dermal/inhalation) toxicity is required on the label and safety data sheet in such cases; see appendices on Allocation of Label Elements and Safety Data Sheets. If the total concentration of relevant unknown-toxicity ingredients is ≤10% then formula in A.1.3.6.1 must be used and corrected to adjust for the percentage of the unknown ingredients as specified in A.1.3.6.2.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: skin corrosion vs skin irritation
rubrics_metrics.description: Skin corrosion: production of irreversible damage to the skin (visible necrosis through epidermis into dermis). Skin irritation: production of reversible damage to the skin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions (A.2.1.1) set the endpoints used for classification; classification should consider all relevant information and test methods as described in subsequent sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered approach for skin corrosion/irritation evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: A tiered approach organizes available information into levels/tiers and provides structured decision-making; classification results directly when information consistently satisfies criteria, otherwise weight-of-evidence within tiers or overall is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See A.2.2.7 and Figure A.2.1. Use human and animal data first, followed by in vitro/ex vivo data, then other animal data and other sources. When information within a tier is inconsistent, apply weight of evidence within that tier. If different tiers conflict, generally give higher-tier information greater weight unless a lower-tier would result in a stricter classification and there's concern for misclassification — then use an overall weight-of-evidence approach. Only adequate and reliable data of sufficient quality should be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin corrosion/irritation categories and sub-categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances are allocated to Category 1 (skin corrosion) or Category 2 (skin irritation). Category 1 may be subdivided into 1A, 1B, 1C when data permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrosive substances should be classified in Category 1 where sub-categorization is not required or data are insufficient. When data are sufficient, assign sub-categories 1A, 1B, or 1C according to Table A.2.1 criteria (based on exposure duration and observation times).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and use of human data for skin classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing reliable and good-quality human data on skin corrosion/irritation should be given high weight for classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human data could be from occupational, consumer, transport, emergency response scenarios, epidemiological and clinical studies, well-documented case reports and observations. Absence of incidents is not evidence for no classification because exposures may be unknown or uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard animal test data for skin corrosion/irritation
rubrics_metrics.description: OECD TG 404 is the standard animal test for skin corrosive/irritant classification; current version uses a maximum of 3 animals. Results from earlier versions are also considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skin corrosion: destructive necrosis through epidermis into dermis in at least one tested animal after initial exposure up to 4 hours (see Table A.2.1). Skin irritation: reversible damage after application up to 4 hours (see Table A.2.2). Use observation periods and scoring as specified in OECD TG 404 and tables A.2.1/A.2.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal criteria for skin corrosion (sub-categories 1A/1B/1C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sub-categories defined by exposure/observation timing for corrosive responses in at least one animal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.2.1: Category 1 = destruction of skin tissue, visible necrosis in at least one animal after exposure ≤4 h. Sub-category 1A: corrosive responses ≤3 min during observation period ≤1 h. 1B: >3 min ≤1 h with observations ≤14 days. 1C: >1 h ≤4 h with observations ≤14 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal criteria for skin irritation (Category 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for irritant classification based on mean scores or persistent inflammation and allowances for variability among animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.2.2: Irritant (Category 2) criteria include: (1) Mean score of ≥2.3 ≤4.0 for erythema/eschar or for edema in at least 2 of 3 tested animals from gradings at 24, 48, 72 hours after patch removal (or delayed reactions as specified); or (2) inflammation persisting to end of observation period (normally 14 days) with hyperplasia and scaling; or (3) in cases of pronounced variability, pronounced effects in a single animal may be sufficient if clearly related to exposure. Grading criteria per OECD TG 404.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of in vitro/ex vivo data for skin classification
rubrics_metrics.description: In vitro/ex vivo methods address either skin irritation or skin corrosion, not both in a single test; classification from such data requires methods validated/accepted and substances to be within applicability domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internationally validated/accepted in vitro/ex vivo test methods where possible and apply their classification criteria. For corrosion, OECD TGs 430, 431, 435 can be used to classify Category 1 (and sub-categories where possible); where methods cannot distinguish sub-categories, take additional information into account or apply Category 1. For irritation, OECD TG 439 can be used to classify Category 2. Negative results from validated tests can support 'not classified' conclusions if within applicability domain. Consider limitations and applicability domains described in test methods and literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of other existing animal skin data
rubrics_metrics.description: Other animal data may be used for classification, but may have limitations depending on systemic toxicity and test conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations of corrosion/irritation in acute toxicity studies may be used if dilutions and species are relevant. Solid substances may become corrosive/irritant when moistened; standardized test methods indicate this. Consider limitations when dermal toxicity prevents a dedicated in vivo study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification based on chemical properties (pH rule) for skin
rubrics_metrics.description: pH extremes such as ≤2 and ≥11.5 may indicate skin corrosion and, in absence of other information, a substance is considered corrosive (Skin Category 1) at these pH values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider acid/alkaline reserve (buffering capacity); if buffering suggests substance may not be corrosive despite extreme pH, confirm with other data, preferably an appropriate validated in vitro/ex vivo test. Buffering capacity and pH may be determined by methods including OECD TG 122.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification using non-test methods for skin
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-test methods (computer SAR, QSAR, expert systems, read-across) may be used case-by-case with due consideration of reliability and applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read-across requires sufficiently reliable test data on similar substances and justification of similarity; read-across generally has higher weight than (Q)SARs when adequately justified. (Q)SARs require sufficient data and validation of the model per internationally recognized principles. Lack of alerts in a SAR/expert system is not sufficient evidence for no classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered approach details and weight-of-evidence rules for skin
rubrics_metrics.description: How to organize information across tiers and apply weight-of-evidence where data are inconsistent or conflicting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order of tiers (Figure A.2.1): existing human and animal data highest, then in vitro/ex vivo data, other existing animal data, then other sources. If data within a tier conflict, determine conclusion by weight of evidence within that tier. If tiers conflict, higher-tier info generally given greater weight, except when a lower tier would result in a stricter classification and misclassification concern exists — then determine by overall weight of evidence. Only adequate and reliable data of sufficient quality should be included. Examples of inconclusive information reasons are provided (insufficient quality, inadequate to conclude, unsuitable test method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of mixtures when complete mixture data are available (skin)
rubrics_metrics.description: When data exist for the complete mixture, classify using the criteria for substances and the tiered approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same tiered evaluation as for substances (Figure A.2.1). If in vitro/ex vivo methods were not validated using mixtures, they may still be broadly applicable but only when all ingredients fall within applicability domains and method limitations are considered. In absence of other information, a mixture is considered corrosive (Skin Category 1) if pH ≤2 or ≥11.5 unless acid/alkaline reserve suggests otherwise; confirm with validated in vitro tests where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principles for mixtures when mixture not tested
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the mixture itself has not been tested but sufficient data exist on individual ingredients and similar tested mixtures, use bridging principles to characterize hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridging principles (A.0.5) include: Dilution, Batching, Concentration of mixtures, Interpolation within one hazard category, Substantially similar mixtures, and Aerosols. Use these principles where appropriate to infer mixture hazard from ingredient/similar mixture data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'relevant ingredients' for mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant ingredients of a mixture are those present in concentrations ≥1% (w/w for solids/liquids/dusts/mists/vapors; v/v for gases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the classifier has reason to suspect an ingredient present at <1% will affect classification for skin corrosion/irritation, that ingredient must also be considered relevant. This definition applies for tiered approaches to ingredient-based classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity theory and weighting factor for mixtures (skin)
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying mixtures based on ingredient data, use the theory of additivity: each corrosive or irritant ingredient contributes in proportion to potency and concentration; apply a weighting factor of 10 for corrosive ingredients present below the concentration limit for Category 1 but that may contribute to irritant classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the mixture as corrosive or irritant when the sum of concentrations (after weighting where specified) exceeds cut-off values/concentration limits provided in Table A.2.3. Particular care for classes of chemicals (strong acids/bases, inorganic salts, aldehydes, phenols, surfactants) where additivity approach may not apply and pH or other criteria should be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut-off concentration limits for mixture classification (skin) — Table A.2.3
rubrics_metrics.description: Table A.2.3 provides the cut-off value/concentration limits to determine if the mixture is considered corrosive or irritant to the skin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text from table: 'Table A.2.3—Concentration of Ingredients of a Mixture Classified as Skin Category 1 or 2 That Would Trigger Classification of the Mixture as Hazardous to Skin [Category 1 or 2] Sum of ingredients classified as: Concentration triggering classification of a mixture as: Skin corrosive Skin irritant Category 1 Category 2 Skin Category 1 ≥5% ≥1% but <5% Skin Category 2 ≥10% (10 × Skin Category 1) + Skin Category 2 ≥10%'. Note: where sub-categories 1A/1B/1C used, sums for each sub-category must meet ≥5% rules for sub-categorization; rules on combining sub-category sums to determine resulting sub-category are provided in the note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures where additivity does not apply — Table A.2.4
rubrics_metrics.description: Special concentration triggers for mixtures when the additivity approach does not apply (e.g., acids/bases/inorganics/aldehydes/phenols/surfactants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.2.4 text: 'Ingredient — Concentration (percent) — Mixture classified as: Skin: Acid with pH ≤2 — ≥1 — Category 1. Base with pH ≥11.5 — ≥1 — Category 1. Other corrosive (Category 1) ingredient — ≥1 — Category 1. Other irritant (Category 2) ingredient, including acids and bases — ≥ 3 — Category 2.' Also: For mixtures containing corrosive/irritant ingredients that cannot be classified by additivity, classify as Category 1 if contains ≥1% corrosive ingredient and Category 2 when contains ≥3% irritant ingredient. Use cut-off values/concentration limits guidance (A.0.4.3) and consider testing if reliable data indicate effects will not be evident above generic cut-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: serious eye damage vs eye irritation
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious eye damage: tissue damage in the eye or serious decay of vision not fully reversible after exposure. Eye irritation: changes in the eye that are fully reversible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions (A.3.1.1) set endpoints for eye hazard classification and are used in the tiered approach described in A.3.1.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered approach for serious eye damage/eye irritation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a tiered approach emphasizing existing human data first, then animal data, then validated in vitro tests, and then other information; apply weight-of-evidence when direct criteria cannot be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all available information including validated in vitro tests, relevant animal data, and human data (epidemiological, clinical studies, case reports). Where criteria cannot be directly applied, make classification based on total weight of evidence (A.0.3.1). Avoid unnecessary animal testing; consider skin corrosion potential prior to eye testing to avoid inappropriate testing of skin corrosive substances on eyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eye damage/irritation categories and animal test criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances allocated to Category 1 (serious eye damage/irreversible effects) or Category 2 (eye irritation/reversible effects). Category 2 may be further split into 2A (effects reverse within ~21 days) and 2B (within ~7 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table A.3.1: Category 1 criteria include effects in at least one animal not expected to reverse within ~21 days and/or in at least 2 of 3 animals corneal opacity ≥3 and/or iritis >1.5 (mean scores at 24, 48, 72 h) as described in OECD TG 405. Table A.3.2: Category 2/2A criteria: in at least 2 of 3 animals positive responses of corneal opacity ≥1 and/or iritis ≥1 and/or conjunctival redness ≥2 and/or conjunctival oedema ≥2, fully reverses within ~21 days; 2B if reversible within 7 days. Account for pronounced variability among animal responses when determining classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiered approach specifics and validated in vitro tests for eye damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use validated in vitro alternatives to make classification decisions where available; pH extremes (≤2 or ≥11.5) may indicate serious eye damage but consider buffering capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of validated tests for identifying eye corrosives/severe irritants include OECD TGs 437 (BCOP), 438 (ICE), and 460 (FL). Presently there are no validated internationally accepted in vitro methods for identifying eye irritation. A positive validated in vitro test for skin corrosion may lead to classification as causing serious eye damage. Measurement of pH alone may be adequate, but assessment of acid/alkaline reserve (buffering capacity) is preferable (no validated method currently). Negative results from applicable validated in vitro tests are considered in the total weight-of-evidence evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of mixtures for serious eye damage/eye irritation — complete mixture data
rubrics_metrics.description: If data are available for the complete mixture, classify using substance criteria and the tiered approach (Figure A.3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing mixtures, use tiered approach to ensure accurate classification and avoid unnecessary animal testing. In absence of other information, a mixture with pH ≤2 or ≥11.5 is considered to cause serious eye damage (Category 1) unless acid/alkaline reserve suggests otherwise; further evaluation (preferably validated in vitro) may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging and additivity principles for eye-damaging mixtures when mixture not tested
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mixture hasn't been tested but sufficient ingredient and similar mixture data exist, use bridging principles and an additivity approach to classify serious eye damage/eye irritation hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bridging principles (dilution, batching, concentration of mixtures, interpolation within one hazard category, substantially similar mixtures, aerosols). Define relevant ingredients as those ≥1% (v/v or w/w); consider <1% if suspected to affect classification. Apply additivity: each corrosive or serious eye damaging/eye irritant ingredient contributes proportionally to potency and concentration; apply a weighting factor of 10 for skin corrosive and serious eye damaging ingredients present below concentration limits that may contribute to eye irritancy. Classify when sum of concentrations exceeds cut-off values in Table A.3.3. For acids/bases/inorganics/aldehydes/phenols/surfactants, additivity may not apply; for strong acids/bases use pH as the classification criterion. If additivity approach cannot be applied, classify as Category 1 if contains ≥1% skin corrosive/serious eye damaging ingredient and Category 2 if ≥3% eye irritant ingredient. Consider testing if reliable data suggest ingredient effects won't be evident above generic cut-offs.
